name: Jamal Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. Tell me about a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jamal Schmidt, 43, and I'm a junior hand on building sites. I left school early and I'm still learning carpentry; I carry materials, set out fixings, and sometimes cut pieces under the lead's eye. I use an AI tool on my phone every day to turn his rough list into a checklist, but I trust his pencil mark before I cut. I like making something the children can point to; I hate holding up the crew when I measure twice and still get it wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is home like at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nia works shifts at a laundry, and our children are eight and eleven. We have a mortgage, less than a month's expenses saved, and my pay is near the bottom on site. There aren't many other crews hiring nearby, so even a week without wages makes the next payment tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads that the phone is a handy list, not a pair of hands. I'd also tell them a steady job matters more to me than arguing over whether AI is clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the building work still needs us, but our mortgage is already close to the edge each month. A rainy week or a job ending scares me more than a small change to paperwork, and my low place on the crew gives me little say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep showing up for the early shift and use my phone checklist to avoid missing fixings. In the first year I'd ask our lead to show me one new joint each week, then practise on offcuts after the paid work is done; I won't spend the grocery money on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even in the mild picture. The mortgage does not wait for a technology story to become dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes short in a bad week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop buying takeaway food and postpone replacing the children's shoes if they can still wear the old ones. I don't want to touch the mortgage payment; that's why I count the days on the calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the checklist really help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday it reminded me to bring the right fixings upstairs before the plasterer arrived. It saves my legs and sometimes saves the lead from calling me back down.

say: I would call the AI phone tool a **handy list**, while stressing steady paid work.
I would keep talking about the **crew**, not big predictions.
think: My **mortgage** is tight before any AI change.
My **junior position** and scarce local openings make lost hours hard to replace.
do: Keep arriving for the **early shift** and using the checklist.
Practise one **new joint** weekly on offcuts after paid work.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary wage gaps and the mortgage.
S0.quote: The mortgage does not wait for a technology story to become dramatic.
fieldNote: Jamal uses **AI daily** for a narrow checklist, but sees the bigger threat in an ordinary missed wage.
His **thin savings** and few nearby openings make even the plateau uncomfortable despite construction continuing.

steps.text: Keep taking early paid shifts on the current building crew
Use the AI phone checklist to bring correct fixings upstairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can send us a better list, but it cannot fix a bowed door frame for us yet. I'd ask whoever writes the new schedule to put an actual fitter on the call before setting a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning jobs may go first, but bosses could then demand faster site work with fewer people. I'm the least experienced hand, so I could lose shifts if the crew gets smaller; Nia's laundry shifts are not enough to carry the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask my lead to teach me door hanging, and I'd use the AI tool to make a picture checklist of each step. In the first year I'd apply for any paid helper opening with the two repair firms I can reach by bus if our shifts begin dropping; I will keep working here meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn quickly. Learning doesn't pay the mortgage until somebody pays me to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why those repair firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One takes small household jobs and the other does insurance repairs. I have seen their vans near the bus stop, so I know I can get there without buying a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Nia if our rota drops below four days, then we'd cut the weekend trips first. We can manage a small dip, but not months of it.

say: I would ask for a **fitter** to check software schedules before deadlines.
I would remind coworkers that **bowed frames** still require site work.
think: I could lose **paid shifts** if a faster schedule shrinks the crew.
My partner’s **laundry wages** cannot carry the mortgage alone.
do: Learn **door hanging** with the lead and build a picture checklist.
Apply to two **repair firms** if site shifts start falling.
Keep working **current shifts** while testing other openings.
feel: **Anxious** about a smaller rota and a tight mortgage.
S1.quote: Learning doesn't pay the mortgage until somebody pays me to use it.
fieldNote: His concern centres on his **junior place** in a crew that may be trimmed even before physical robots arrive.
He links learning to **paid openings** reachable by bus, rather than assuming a new skill produces wages automatically.

steps.text: Build an AI picture checklist while learning door hanging from the lead
Apply to two bus-accessible repair firms if shifts begin falling
Keep paid shifts on current crew during the job search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew that 2028 changes the drawings and orders first, and 2031 brings robots onto the tools if this comes true. I won't pretend a phone makes me safe just because I know its menus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AGI handles planning in two years, the lead may need fewer hours from a junior who still makes cutting mistakes. Once robots do the lifting and fitting around 2031, I expect my site wage could disappear. Our savings will barely cover one mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the repair firms about paid apprentice-style work in leak repair, even though I'm 43, and apply if they offer wages while teaching. In 2029 I'd keep site shifts and use AGI checklists on repairs, but I would also ask the lender about a payment plan the week my hours are cut, not after we miss a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have children in school and a mortgage due every month, and the robot date comes before I can build much cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would leak repair be safe after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No trade is a promise if robots can use their hands as well as ours. I hope cramped old houses take longer to automate, but I'd want paid trials to prove there is work, not just my guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the children hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children we are staying in the house as long as we can make the payments. I wouldn't put the debt on them, but I'd explain why trips and extra treats are on hold.

say: I would warn that **2028 AGI** changes plans before **2031 robots** reach site work.
I would tell the crew my **phone skills** do not guarantee a job.
think: My **junior wage** could shrink when planning work changes.
I expect my **site income** may disappear when robots can fit and lift.
do: Apply for **paid leak-repair training** if a repair firm offers it.
Keep **site shifts** in 2029 and use AGI checklists on repairs.
Contact the **mortgage lender** as soon as hours are cut.
feel: **Alarmed** by an expected wage loss before savings can grow.
S2.quote: Our savings will barely cover one mortgage payment.
fieldNote: The fast timeline exposes both his **junior hours** and later physical tasks while the mortgage leaves almost no buffer.
He is willing to enter **paid training** at 43, but makes the wage condition explicit and has a lender plan.

steps.text: Apply for paid leak-repair training if a local firm offers wages
Keep earning site wages through 2029 while possible
Use AGI checklists on repair tasks in 2029
Ask mortgage lender for a payment plan when hours first fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew there are five years before the planning change and about eight before the robots, so we have time to learn more than one kind of repair. I'd still want a date on the rota next week, not a talk about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, I may lose junior site hours when AGI does layouts and ordering, but fitting should still need people until about 2034. At 51, robots could take the work I finally learned; without more savings or a different paid role, the mortgage would still be a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our lead for paid time on bathroom repairs this year, then keep a log of jobs where I worked without being called back. By 2032 I'd apply for a maintenance crew position at the local housing office if it is hiring; in the first year after 2031 I'd use AGI to organise callouts but check each leak in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More time means I can gain a track record, but my pay is too low to sit back for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a housing maintenance crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The housing office owns old flats that always have loose taps and damaged doors. I could get there by bus, but I don't know whether they'll have a vacancy, so I'd keep asking rather than count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lead will not give you bathroom work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a paid Saturday job with a repair firm if they will supervise me. I can't donate weekday wages for experience, because the mortgage takes most of them.

say: I would tell coworkers the **2031 planning** change comes before **2034 robots**.
I would insist that next week’s **rota** still matters.
think: My **junior hours** could fall in 2031 as layouts move to AGI.
My **repair wage** may be threatened again when robots reach hands-on work.
do: Ask for **paid bathroom repairs** and record completed jobs.
Apply for **housing maintenance** work by 2032 if hiring.
Use **AGI callout lists** while inspecting leaks in person after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about low pay, with time to build a record.
S3.quote: I can't donate weekday wages for experience, because the mortgage takes most of them.
fieldNote: He sees five extra years as a chance to build **paid repair experience**, not as an excuse to stop earning.
The possible **housing-office vacancy** is uncertain; he plans applications without treating it as a guaranteed refuge from robots.

steps.text: Ask lead for paid bathroom repair shifts and log finished jobs
Apply for housing maintenance vacancy by 2032 if hiring
Use AGI to organise callouts after 2031 while checking leaks
Keep current paid site shifts while building repair experience

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives my children time to finish school and me time to become a dependable tradesman. But I'll be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036 and 56 when the robots come about 2039, and I cannot treat that as retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child will be 21 and the younger 18 by 2036, so their daily school costs should change, though they may need help starting out. The mortgage might still be there; I expect site work to narrow after 2039 and I need wages beyond that, not a hopeful story about old hands being special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd set aside a small fixed amount after each pay packet, even if it's only ten, and practise repairs on paid jobs. In 2037 I'd use AGI for material lists while applying for maintenance posts; in the first year after 2036 I'd review the mortgage balance with Nia before deciding whether we need a cheaper home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less trapped than in the two-year picture. Ten years gives me a chance to save and prove I can do repairs, if work holds long enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the older child to earn instead of studying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd want our older child to choose a path with a wage at the end, whether that's college or an apprenticeship. I won't pretend their school costs last forever, but I don't know what help they might need at 21.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save such a small amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten comes out of a lower wage without taking the food money. If I can hold it for a year, that's a start; I'd raise it only when the mortgage and groceries are covered.

say: I would say the **decade** lets me build a reliable trade record.
I would point out that **56** is too young to count on retirement.
think: My children’s **school costs** will change as they become adults.
I still expect **site wages** to narrow after 2039 robots.
do: Set aside **ten** from each pay packet after bills.
Keep practising **paid repairs** and apply for maintenance roles by 2037.
Review the **mortgage balance** with Nia after AGI arrives.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to save and build a record gradually.
S4.quote: I need wages beyond that, not a hopeful story about old hands being special.
fieldNote: He correctly ages his children and himself, seeing **adult children** without assuming they become costless or dependent forever.
A small **savings habit** fits his low pay; he still expects to need work when robots reach sites.

steps.text: Set aside ten from each pay packet after mortgage and groceries
Practise repair skills on paid building jobs over the decade
Keep earning current site wages while building a work record

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture. I could lose the little margin we have before I get good enough at repairs to be hired for them, and by 2031 the robots could take the fitting jobs. Paid training with a local repair firm and a mortgage payment plan if my hours drop would help us stay afloat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a person learns a trade at my age without missing wages. I can practise at night, but my children need me home too. If a contractor wants new skills, the learning has to happen on paid hours somewhere.

headlineQuote: If a contractor wants new skills, the learning has to happen on paid hours somewhere.
portrait: Jamal is a **43-year-old junior** construction hand, still learning after leaving school early.
A **mortgage**, two school-age children and less than one month saved make even ordinary lost hours threatening.
He uses **AI daily** for checklists and seeks paid repair skills rather than unpaid certificates.
He expects **2031 robots** to threaten site wages and asks for paid training and lender help.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** threatens his narrow wage margin before he can qualify for repair work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid repair training** and a mortgage payment plan would let his household survive a fall in site hours.
